Q: How to generate PowerShell Module with TypeSpec from OpenAPI? A:

Note: The following is an educated guess, based on consulting the docs only, and is a high-level overview only:

  • TypeSpec is a protocol-agnostic DSL inspired by TypeScript for (typically web-service) API design.

    • As such, it is appealing to developers already familiar with TypeScript / JavaScript and the Node.js/npm ecosystem.

  • What TypeSpec emits (compiles to), via an extensible plug-in system called emitters, are API specifications - e.g., in OpenAPI format - rather than code in implementation languages such as PowerShell.

    • It is at the level of the resulting specifications that code generators are available.

The upshot for PowerShell is:

  • You'll need to learn the TypeSpec DSL in order to design your APIs.
    While existing knowledge of TypeScript is the easiest way in, it shouldn't take too long to start from scratch, given that the DSL is limited in scope and syntax.

  • Once you compile a design to a given specification, say OpenAPI, you can use a PowerShell code generator on it, such as the OpenAPI PowerShell generator (note: marked as beta as of this writing).

Q: fetching from an API in react A:

When you fetch data in React using useEffect, it can work — but it’s very easy to introduce subtle bugs:

  • Duplicate requests (especially in development).

  • Re-fetching because of unstable dependencies.

  • Extra guards using useRef to prevent multiple calls.

  • Edge cases when state goes from null → 0 or similar transitions.

  • Manual handling of loading, error, retry, caching, and refetch logic.

You can patch these issues with careful dependency management and additional checks, but the complexity grows quickly. The more dynamic your component becomes, the more fragile this pattern can feel.

That’s exactly the problem @tanstack/react-query is designed to solve.

Why useQuery is more robust

Using useQuery:

  • Automatically deduplicates requests.

  • Caches responses.

  • Handles background refetching.

  • Prevents unnecessary refetches when switching tabs.

  • Manages loading and error states cleanly.

  • Gives you retry logic and stale-time control out of the box.

Instead of manually orchestrating all of that with useEffect, you describe what data you need and React Query handles how and when to fetch it.

Is it more “professional” to use it everywhere?

For server-state (data coming from an API), yes — using React Query is generally considered best practice in modern React applications.

For example, in something like AddProduct.tsx:

  • If you are fetching categories, tags, or existing product data → useQuery is a great fit.

  • If you are submitting a form → useMutation is the correct abstraction.

Where you shouldn’t use it:

  • Pure local UI state.

  • Derived values.

  • Static data that never changes.

About server-side usage

React Query can absolutely work with SSR (Next.js, etc.), but you need hydration/dehydration setup. That’s not a limitation — it just requires extra configuration.

Short Answer

Yes — for API fetching, especially in real-world applications, using TanStack Query is more scalable, cleaner, and less error-prone than manually managing useEffect everywhere.

useEffect is fine for simple side effects.

React Query is better for managing server state.

That’s the architectural distinction.

Q: Now that `finalize()` is deprecated in Java, what should be used instead, especially for a global singleton? A:

Java 9 introduces the Cleaner and Cleanable utility classes which take care of wiring up phantom references to a queue and a cleaning thread draining that queue.

While this lets you separate out the witness that will perform a post-mortem cleanup after the owning object has died, all the caveats about GC-triggered resource management still apply, i.e. it is still preferable to rely on AutoClosable and try-with-resources blocks to manage the lifecycle of resources, not on the garbage collector.

Q: Visual Studio Code + Spring Boot Project change spring.properties.additional-location etc A:

Or you can download Spring Boot Dashboard which is currently in preview.

First, it's needed to adjust your naming to the properties file to sth like application-{profile}.properties, not like {profile}.properties.

And go to the Spring Boot Dashboard tab, and then right click on the application shown in the APPS section. Click on Run/Debug with profile button, and then enter the profile name--local. If your properties file is called application-local.properties, it should be no problem.
